claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by a thermally activated, rate-dependent dislocation mechanism.
Increasing temperature and strain rate cause FeNiCrMn to transition from predominantly glide-controlled deformation to deformation increasingly influenced by climb or cross-slip.
Strong solute-dislocation interactions are inherent to the Co-free FeNiCrMn system and modulate the activation barrier for dislocation motion.
The proposed dislocation-mechanism transition underpins the maintained strength-ductility balance of FeNiCrMn.
The initial alloy is equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn in an as-cast, single-phase state.
The as-cast FeNiCrMn microstructure is homogeneous and contains inherent dislocations and defects.
Temperature and strain rate affect the dynamic response of related high-entropy alloys.
Massive dislocation nucleation and drag have been associated with increased strain-rate sensitivity in CrCoFeNi.
At lower temperatures and strain rates, dislocation glide predominates in FeNiCrMn and provides high strength through organized slip.
Increasing temperature supplies thermal energy that enhances dislocation mobility through climb or cross-slip.
Increasing strain rate, together with increasing temperature, promotes climb or cross-slip in FeNiCrMn.
The controlled study will vary temperature from room temperature to about 800 K and strain rate from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 under isothermal tensile or compression loading.
TEM and strain-rate-sensitivity analysis will be used to measure dislocation density, slip-mode features, and activation volume.
The hypothesized transition should produce an inflection or regime shift in strain-rate sensitivity or activation volume that coincides with TEM evidence of changed dislocation mode.
Under quasi-static room-temperature conditions, glide is the primary plastic-deformation mode and the FeNiCrMn strength-ductility balance is firmly established.
Twinning, grain-boundary mechanisms, diffusion creep, dynamic recrystallization, and adiabatic shear banding can contribute to deformation in high-entropy alloys.

The proposed mechanism is bounded to room temperature through about 800 K and strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1, and may not be observable where twinning, dynamic recrystallization, or adiabatic shear banding dominates.
Similar high- and medium-entropy-alloy data support a glide-to-climb-or-cross-slip transition.
The hypothesis is falsified if neither an inflection in strain-rate sensitivity or activation volume nor a corresponding TEM-observed mechanism change occurs over the tested regimes.
